title: Cells Release Energy Stored in Sugar

scenes.tts: Pack sprouting peas into a thermos. A day or two later, the thermometer can climb above room temperature. Boiled peas in another thermos stay close to the room. Peas have no muscles. So where does the warmth come from?
scenes.visual: Two thermos blocks with thermometers; the sprouting-pea thermometer rises above the room line, the boiled-pea one does not; question appears.
scenes.narration: Pack sprouting peas into a thermos. A day or two later, the thermometer can climb above room temperature. Boiled peas in another thermos stay close to the room. Peas have no muscles. So where does the warmth come from?

scenes.tts: A pea seed stores energy in its molecules. The fuel this lesson follows is glucose, a sugar that stores energy. Plants make glucose by photosynthesis. Cells must break food down to use its energy.
scenes.visual: A seed block holds sugar chips; glucose highlighted; photosynthesis arrow brings glucose in; cell block breaks it down.
scenes.narration: A pea seed stores energy in its molecules. The fuel this lesson follows is glucose, a sugar that stores energy. Plants make glucose by photosynthesis. Cells must break food down to use its energy.

scenes.tts: Cells do this by cellular respiration. Cellular respiration is how cells break down sugar with oxygen and release energy. Sugar and oxygen go in. Carbon dioxide and water come out, along with the released energy. Oxygen is a gas in the air that cells use. Carbon dioxide is a gas that cells give off.
scenes.visual: Glucose and oxygen chips flow into a respiration box; carbon dioxide, water and energy chips flow out.
scenes.narration: Cells do this by cellular respiration. Cellular respiration is how cells break down sugar with oxygen and release energy. Sugar and oxygen go in. Carbon dioxide and water come out, along with the released energy. Oxygen is a gas in the air that cells use. Carbon dioxide is a gas that cells give off.

scenes.tts: Most of this happens in small parts of the cell called mitochondria. One is a mitochondrion. A mitochondrion is an organelle where cells release energy from food. Plant cells and animal cells both have them. Almost all plant, animal and fungus cells have mitochondria.
scenes.visual: An animal cell outline with green mitochondria, one labelled; a plant cell outline with mitochondria appears beside it.
scenes.narration: Most of this happens in small parts of the cell called mitochondria. One is a mitochondrion. A mitochondrion is an organelle where cells release energy from food. Plant cells and animal cells both have them. Almost all plant, animal and fungus cells have mitochondria.

scenes.tts: The cell spends some of the released energy on work. One kind of work is building new cell parts. Some energy always leaves as thermal energy. Thermal energy is the energy of moving particles, which you feel as warmth. The energy was already stored in the sugar. Respiration changes its form.
scenes.visual: Energy stored in sugar splits by two arrows into cell work and thermal energy with jiggling particles.
scenes.narration: The cell spends some of the released energy on work. One kind of work is building new cell parts. Some energy always leaves as thermal energy. Thermal energy is the energy of moving particles, which you feel as warmth. The energy was already stored in the sugar. Respiration changes its form.

scenes.tts: Now the two thermoses make sense. Sprouting peas are alive, so their cells respire. Some released energy leaves as thermal energy, and the thermos holds it in. Boiled peas are dead, so they do not respire. Plants, fungi and animals all respire. Breathing is moving air in and out of your lungs. It is not the same as respiration. Respiration happens inside cells. Your cells use oxygen to release the energy stored in sugar.
scenes.visual: Thermos pair returns with alive/respires and dead/no respiration; breathing and respiration compared; final answer line.
